# Chapter 6 · Boundaries and the Future: Compliance, Industries, and the Next Paradigm

## 86. Who actually owns the copyright on content generated by large models?

The copyright question around model-generated content is a legal gray zone every AI product must face on its way to commercialization. The reality today is that no major jurisdiction has given a clear answer. The US Copyright Office leans toward the view that purely AI-generated content gets no copyright protection, because copyright law protects the creativity of a human author. Chinese courts have reached inconsistent rulings across several cases when deciding whether AI-generated content qualifies for copyright.

This ambiguity creates real risk for products, and it surfaces from two directions. One direction is infringement liability. When a user puts a model-generated image, piece of copy, or block of code to commercial use and that content infringes a third party's copyright, the lines of responsibility blur into a mess: the user says the product generated it, the product says the user triggered it, the third party says both should pay. The other direction is the difficulty of enforcement. When a third party copies the product's high-quality generated content, the user who wants to enforce finds they have no copyright because the content is AI-generated, and the product that wants to enforce finds it is not the author either. Both sides are stuck.

What the PM must do is write copyright risk into the product design and the user agreement. At the product level, avoid generating obviously infringing works, for example by not letting the model directly produce close approximations of known characters, known brands, or known works. At the user-agreement level, spell out copyright ownership and disclaimer clauses: who owns the copyright on generated content, who bears the risk when the user uses it, and under what circumstances the product is exempt. Skip either layer and copyright risk hangs over the product like a sword that, when it falls, spares no one.

## 87. What is the biggest difference between EU/US compliance and Chinese compliance for AI products going overseas?

An AI product going overseas has to deal with two completely different compliance systems at once: one for China, another for the EU and US. Mix them up and the product can get taken down in one market and fined in another. The biggest difference is in regulatory logic.

The core of Chinese compliance is content safety. Generated content must align with mainstream values and must not contain politically sensitive, pornographic, violent, or rumor-based violations. A content-safety assessment is required before launch and continuous monitoring after. The core of EU/US compliance is data protection and algorithm transparency. GDPR imposes strict rules on the collection, use, and storage of user data. AI acts impose explicit requirements on algorithm transparency, explainability, and risk assessment. The two logics shape product design in entirely different ways. For Chinese compliance, the focus is content filtering and safety review, which means investing in content recognition, violation interception, and incident response. For EU/US compliance, the focus is data governance and algorithm documentation, which means investing in data desensitization, user authorization, and algorithm explainability.

An overseas product must satisfy both systems. Picking one and dropping the other is impossible; both must be done. Costs will rise, of course, but compliance is cheaper done early than late. After a product launches overseas, the loss from fines and takedowns far outweighs the upfront investment.

## 88. Where exactly is the compliance red line on using user data for model training?

Whether user data can feed model training is one of the most sensitive compliance questions for AI products. Where the red line sits depends on the jurisdiction. China's Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) requires consent to process personal information, and separate consent for sensitive personal information. The Generative AI Service Management Measures go further, requiring that user data used for training be disclosed to users and authorized. The EU's GDPR is stricter still: using user data for training requires explicit disclosure of the purpose, explicit user consent, the user's right to withdraw consent at any time, and the user's right to demand deletion of data already used for training. The US has no unified federal law yet, but state-level laws like California's CCPA already carry similar requirements.

Local rules differ in detail, but the red line boils down to three rules. Disclosure is the first: whether user data will be used for training must be stated clearly to the user, not buried in a lengthy privacy policy. Consent is the second: using user data for training requires the user's explicit consent, not a pre-checked default box. Withdrawability is the third: the user can withdraw consent at any time, and data already used for training must be handled so that at minimum it is not used going forward. Fail any of these three and you are over the line. Domestic regulation is tightening and overseas fines routinely run into astronomical figures; do it on hope and it will blow up sooner or later.

## 89. After the Generative AI Service Management Measures took effect, how should a PM build a compliance checklist that actually passes review?

The Generative AI Service Management Measures came into force in August 2023. Providing generative AI services now requires a safety assessment, an algorithm filing, and content filtering. The PM must fold compliance design into the product's full lifecycle instead of patching it on before launch. The compliance checklist can be advanced in five stages.

At the initiation stage, confirm three things: whether the product falls under the Measures, whether an algorithm filing is required, and roughly how much effort the safety assessment will take. At the design stage, do four things: design a content-safety filtering mechanism (both input and output layers), design an incident-response flow for violating content, design a user feedback and reporting mechanism, and design a safety-review flow for training data. At the development stage, integrate a third-party content-safety service or build your own filtering model, keep source records and legality reviews for training data, and produce algorithm explainability documentation.

At the launch stage, complete the algorithm filing, complete the safety assessment and retain the report, and stand up a content-safety duty roster. At the operations stage, update violation-detection rules periodically, report operational status to the regulator on a regular basis, and build a fast-response mechanism for user complaints. This checklist is not a one-time artifact. Laws update and products iterate, so compliance design must keep updating with them. Teams that treat compliance as a burden eventually get fined into appreciating its value; teams that treat compliance as a moat gain a competitive edge precisely when regulation tightens.

## 90. What is the biggest difference between a financial-industry AI PM and an internet AI PM?

A financial-industry AI PM and an internet AI PM seem to do similar things on the surface, but their underlying logic is completely different. The biggest difference is their attitude toward errors.

The internet AI PM is used to fast iteration, canary releases, and treating real users as the test bed. When something breaks, fix it and ship again. A product with millions of daily active users has high fault tolerance. Finance is nothing like this. A single error can cause customer fund losses, trigger a regulatory investigation, or spark a public-opinion crisis. A financial AI PM's fault tolerance is close to zero. This difference dictates a fundamentally different way of working. When a financial AI PM takes a requirement, the first thing they ask is what could go wrong; every feature needs a risk assessment and every risk needs a response plan. The evaluation system's center of gravity also differs. The internet AI PM looks at user experience and business conversion. The financial AI PM looks at accuracy, compliance, and explainability.

The financial AI PM also faces constraints the internet AI PM never meets. Models must be explainable: regulation requires that financial decisions explain why, and black-box models are unusable in many scenarios. Data isolation is extreme: customer data cannot leave the domain, and model training must happen in an isolated environment. Approval flows are long: a single feature can take months of internal approval and external filing. The core competence of a financial AI PM is less about building AI products than about building them under extreme constraints, and the tighter the constraints, the greater the PM's value.

## 91. Why is educational AI so hard to build, and what is the real moat?

Educational AI looks beautiful from a distance and is brutally hard up close. The difficulty stacks four factors at once.

The first hurdle is hard-to-verify outcomes. Education is a long process; the effect of today's learning shows up months or years later, so whether an AI product works is hard to judge in the short term. The second hurdle is hard-to-achieve personalization. Every student has a different baseline, pace, and learning style. If an AI product cannot personalize deeply, its effect gets crushed by traditional one-on-one teaching. The third hurdle is hard-to-build trust. Parents have low natural trust in AI education products; they worry about their child's eyesight, about the AI teaching wrong things, about the child becoming dependent. These worries are not things technology can solve directly. The fourth hurdle is a hard-to-sustain business model. Consumer-side parents have limited willingness to pay, and institutional-side schools have long procurement cycles. A free model cannot accumulate enough users, and a paid model cannot lift conversion.

The real moat is neither the model nor the content. Everyone can call the same models, and educational content itself is not scarce. The moat is the data flywheel. Every practice session, every mistake, every bit of progress a student makes on the product is unique data. Accumulate it and the model understands each student more deeply and personalizes better. Whoever spins up the data flywheel first gets the moat. Whoever cannot spin it, no matter how strong the model, is just holding a tool.

## 92. How heavy is the "approval" burden for medical AI products, and how should a PM plan for it early?

For medical AI products, approval is the harder gate than technology. Medical AI products are classified by risk level. Low-risk auxiliary tools (hospital management, scheduling systems) have relatively simple approval. Mid-to-high-risk diagnosis assistance and treatment-plan recommendation must obtain a medical device registration certificate, and obtaining one is a long, expensive process.

The flow has three steps. The clinical trial comes first: prospective clinical trials across multiple hospitals to prove safety and efficacy, typically one to two years and millions to tens of millions in cost. Technical review comes second: submit the trial data to the regulator, where experts review the product's technical metrics, clinical value, and risk control. Quality system inspection comes third: the regulator inspects the manufacturer's quality-management system to ensure the product can be produced consistently and stably. The whole process usually takes two to three years and costs tens of millions.

What the PM must do is fold approval into the plan at the initiation stage. At initiation, judge which risk class the product belongs to; mid-to-high-risk products must consider from day one how the clinical trial will run and how the certificate will be obtained. At requirement design, separate which features are diagnosis assistance from which are pure tools: the diagnosis-assistance part goes through the registration flow on its own, while the pure-tool part can launch first, avoiding having the whole product dragged by approval. Skip this planning and you finish the product only to find you must backfill approval, losing at least two years. In two years the market will have already changed.

## 93. Why is 95% recall still not enough for e-commerce AI recommendations, and what is the root cause of "looks relevant but the user won't buy"?

In e-commerce, getting AI recommendation recall to 95% is no longer hard, yet many teams find that higher recall does not lift conversion. Users see the recommendations and simply do not buy. The root cause is that "relevant" and "wants to buy" are two different things.

The underlying logic of recommendation algorithms is similarity. A user views product A, so the algorithm recommends product B, which is similar to A. The basis for similarity is product features, user behavior, and collaborative filtering. But whether the user buys depends on far more than relevance: price, reviews, logistics, brand, and their actual need all matter. A typical case is a user who viewed a certain phone; the algorithm recommends other phones at the same price and specs. They all look relevant, but the user actually wanted the one two hundred cheaper or the one with better reviews. None of the algorithm's recommendations land on the user's real decision point.

To make recommendations actually affect conversion, upgrade from similarity recommendation to decision-point recommendation. The core of decision-point recommendation is understanding what the user weighs most when deciding. Price-sensitive users need recommendations that highlight cost performance. Brand-loyal users need recommendations focused on the same brand. Novelty-seeking users need recommendations that highlight new arrivals. Understanding decision points requires deep mining of user-behavior data: how long they stayed on a product page, which fields they viewed, what they compared, and what they finally bought. Those behaviors hide the decision points. Reaching 95% recall is the starting line. The work from 95% to actually influencing a purchase is more than the work from zero to 95%.

## 94. When large models can generate UI components directly, how should a PM rebuild the prototype-design and requirement-validation flow?

Large models that generate UI components are changing how PMs work. The traditional flow is PM draws a prototype, designer makes it high-fidelity, developer implements it. The chain is long and validation is slow. Now a PM can describe the interface they want and have the model generate an interactive prototype, producing a plan in minutes and iterating multiple versions in hours. This affects PMs far beyond a tool swap; the whole way of working has to be rebuilt.

The rebuild starts with the rhythm of prototype validation. Before, one plan validated per week. Now, five per day. Faster validation means earlier failure and faster convergence. The PM's core competence shifts accordingly, from drawing to describing. Drawing skill is replaced by the tool; describing skill becomes more important. How to put the idea in your head into precise language for the model so it generates what you want becomes the new basic skill. The sample size for requirement validation also changes. Before, one or two plans per requirement. Now, a dozen. More validation means a higher chance of finding the optimal solution. The boundary between PM and designer also rebuilds: the PM can do prototypes alone, and the designer's value moves upstream, toward strategy and systems.

A PM who cannot use large models for prototype design will be replaced by someone who can. This is not alarmism; it is happening.

## 95. Given a product requirement, how do you decide between AI Native and +AI, and how do you draw the decision flow?

For every AI-related product requirement, the PM must first ask one question: should this be AI Native or +AI? AI Native means designing from scratch with AI as the core engine, all functions built around AI capability, and UX fully rebuilt for AI. +AI means adding AI features to an existing product, with AI as an enhancement that does not change the product's core form. Judging which to build looks at three dimensions.

The first dimension is AI's weight in the product's value. If AI is the core value and traditional functions are just support, build AI Native. If traditional functions are the core and AI is just icing, build +AI. The second dimension is usage frequency and scenario. High-frequency use where AI is the main interaction mode fits AI Native; low-frequency use where AI only triggers occasionally fits +AI. The third dimension is team capability and resources. AI Native means building the tech stack, data flywheel, and evaluation system from zero, at huge cost. +AI can reuse the existing architecture at much lower cost.

The decision flow can be drawn like this. First ask whether AI is this product's core value. Yes goes to the AI Native branch; no goes to the +AI branch. The AI Native branch then asks whether the team can support building the AI system from zero. Yes means build AI Native; no means do +AI first to accumulate capability, then consider a rebuild later. The +AI branch then asks whether AI can significantly lift the existing experience. Yes means do +AI; no may mean AI should not be added at all. Judging the direction wrong is the biggest waste: building +AI as AI Native costs enormously for mediocre effect, while building AI Native as +AI buries the product's real value.

## 96. What new capabilities must a multimodal-product PM add?

Multimodality is the next big trend in AI: text, image, audio, and video handled in one model, which fundamentally changes product form. The capabilities a multimodal PM must add go far beyond merely "knowing how to use multimodal models."

Cross-modal interaction design is the most direct new capability. Single-modal products have relatively simple interaction, either text chat or image upload. Multimodal products are far more complex; a user may input text, image, and voice at once, and the model must understand the combined intent. A multimodal evaluation system is the second to add. Single-modal evaluation is relatively mature; multimodal is far more complex. One multimodal output may simultaneously involve text quality, image quality, audio quality, and the consistency among the three. Defining "good" and scoring it are both new problems. A multimodal data flywheel is the third. Single-modal data collection is relatively direct; multimodal collection costs and complexity are much higher. How to collect users' multimodal behavior, how to label it, how to train on it: the whole pipeline must be rebuilt.

Multimodal cost structure is the fourth capability to add. Multimodal token consumption is far higher than pure text; one image may cost tens of times a paragraph, and video even more. The cost structure is completely different, so the pricing model must be redesigned. Multimodal compliance is the fifth. Multimodal content carries far greater compliance risk than pure text. Images can infringe, video can be faked, audio can be used for fraud. Each modality needs its own compliance consideration. These capabilities are not picked up by reading a few articles; they are built by hitting walls, reflecting, and iterating in real projects. Multimodal is the next battlefield, and the earlier the capability building, the better.

## 97. When DeepSeek/Llama catch up to GPT-4 at one-tenth the cost, which product modules should you move from API to local deployment?

Open-source models catching up to closed-source models at an order-of-magnitude lower cost is happening. The decision a PM faces is which modules to move from API to local. The migration criteria look at four dimensions.

Latency sensitivity is the most direct dimension. Latency-sensitive modules gain a large latency cut from local deployment, while latency-insensitive modules are fine with API latency. Data sensitivity is the second dimension. Data-sensitive modules avoid data leaving the domain with local deployment; data-insensitive modules are safe enough with API data security. Call volume is the third dimension. High-volume modules show clear cost advantage locally; low-volume modules are cheaper on API. Effect requirement is the fourth dimension. Extremely high-effect-requirement modules may still need the closed-source model, while medium-requirement modules are fine with open source.

Stacking these four dimensions separates modules into three classes. Must-move-local: high latency sensitivity, high data sensitivity, high call volume, medium effect requirement, such as internal knowledge-base Q&A, customer-service routing, and batch data processing. Must-stay-on-API: low latency sensitivity, low data sensitivity, low call volume, extremely high effect requirement, such as complex reasoning, creative generation, and high-end dialogue. Can-be-hybrid: use API for complex tasks and local for simple tasks, routing each request to a different model by complexity. Migration is not one-and-done; it needs continuous evaluation. Open-source capability is rising and closed-source capability is rising too. Today's optimal choice may need re-selecting in half a year.

## 98. After three years as an AI PM, what was the biggest misjudgment?

Three years into being an AI PM, the easiest pitfalls to hit are usually not technical; they are judgment problems.

The biggest misjudgment is overestimating the importance of the model and underestimating the importance of engineering and data. When first entering the field, PMs easily treat the model as the product's core competitiveness, studying daily which model is stronger, which is cheaper, how to tune prompts for better model performance. Three years in, they realize model capability is a public resource everyone can use the same models; what actually decides product victory is the engineering and data outside the model. On the engineering side, whether fallback mechanisms are well built, whether the evaluation system is tightly constructed, whether the feedback loop spins fast: these are the differentiators. On the data side, whether user-behavior data is fully collected, whether labeling quality is high, whether the flywheel spins fast enough: these are the moat.

Another big misjudgment is treating a demo as a product. In the demo phase the model performs brilliantly, and the PM easily optimistically assumes the product is built. Only at real launch do they find the gap between demo and product is ten times larger than imagined: the demo's cases were hand-picked, while the product faces real users' long-tail problems; the demo needs no fallback, while in the product fallback matters more than the main feature; the demo ignores cost, while in the product cost is a life-or-death line.

A further big misjudgment is underestimating the weight of compliance. Early on, compliance is not taken seriously, assumed to be something only big companies worry about. Three years later, they find that without good compliance, no matter how good the product is, it cannot launch. All three misjudgments are judgment problems. Technical problems can always be solved; a wrong judgment wastes the time window.

## 99. When every company is rushing into Agents, how do you write a report arguing "this scenario should not use an Agent" to convince the boss?

Every company is rushing into Agents, and the boss wants in too, but the PM knows the scenario they own should not use an Agent at all. Convincing the boss is an art. The report's structure has four parts, and the persuasion only lands when they come in order.

At the very front is the scenario description: state the scenario's real need clearly, who the users are, what problem to solve, how it is solved now, and where the pain points are. Next is the Agent-solution analysis: what the solution looks like if an Agent is used to solve it. Be objective; do not deliberately make the Agent option look bad. Then comes the alternative-solution analysis: if not using an Agent, can a simpler solution solve it? Which fits better, a workflow, a rules engine, or traditional ML? Finally, the comparison and conclusion: how the Agent option and the alternative compare on effect, cost, risk, and cycle, what the conclusion is, and what to recommend.

The key to writing this report is to not reject Agents themselves, but to reject their fit in this scenario. The boss wants a judgment; lay out the data and logic and let the boss reach the conclusion. One practical point: the report must always offer an alternative. You cannot just say "should not do it." Saying only that, the boss will think you are lazy. Offering a better solution is what earns trust in your judgment.

## 100. What are AI PMs who have done five full years doing now?

AI PMs with five full years under their belt are the cohort that entered around 2020. They lived through the arc from GPT-3 to GPT-4 to the Agent era, and are among the most senior AI PMs in the industry. They are now spread across four different paths.

One path is staying at a leading AI company to build core products. Most of this group are still at top model and application companies domestically and abroad, owning the definition and evolution of core products. Their core competence is sustained product judgment in a fast-changing technical environment; every model-capability leap forces a fresh judgment of how the product should be built. Another path is driving AI transformation inside a traditional big company. Tencent, Alibaba, ByteDance, and Baidu are all embedding AI into existing businesses, and this group is responsible for landing AI in concrete scenarios. Their core competence is pushing AI projects through complex organizational structures, where coordination, drive, and upward-management skills are as essential as the technology.

Entrepreneurship is the third path. After a few years at a big-company AI PM role, some find the innovation room limited and leave to start their own ventures, building vertical AI tools, industry AI solutions, or AI infrastructure. Their core competence is building product and team from zero to one, requiring business judgment, fundraising, and talent recruiting all at once. Shifting to AI investment or consulting is the fourth path. After accumulating real experience, some find that investment firms and enterprises need AI-literate people to make calls, and move into VC partner or enterprise AI advisor roles. Their core competence is abstracting real experience into judgment frameworks, having seen enough projects and hit enough walls to quickly judge whether a project is sound.

The five-year AI PM's core competence is no longer technical understanding; it is judgment and influence: knowing what to do and what not to, and being able to explain that judgment clearly enough that team and boss believe it. This is the endpoint of the AI PM's five-year evolution, and the starting line of the next five.
